stories.body: More than one million people were moved to safety across eastern China as Typhoon Dolphin made landfall in Zhejiang province with winds of up to 150km/h before weakening into a tropical storm. Wenzhou relocated about 900,000 residents, Shanghai evacuated more than 215,000 people, and Fujian moved nearly 99,000 from high-risk areas. Shanghai cancelled more than 1,300 flights and suspended some transport after a central weather station recorded almost 313mm of rain in 24 hours, its highest such total in more than 150 years; another station recorded nearly 400mm. Authorities warned that heavy rain, flooding and landslide risks would continue through Wednesday across a broad swath of eastern and central China. The storm had previously brought disruption to Taiwan, Okinawa and the Philippines, where monsoon rains intensified by Dolphin were reported to have killed eight people.
stories.headline: China evacuates more than one million people as Typhoon Dolphin brings record rainfall to Shanghai

stories.body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel rejected the US-backed 15-point Gaza plan and that its military would not withdraw until Hamas had undergone what he called genuine, complete disarmament. The plan, advanced by Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, envisages Hamas disarming in exchange for an Israeli withdrawal and an eventual transition to a Palestinian governing body; it initially focuses on heavy weapons, military sites, depots and tunnels. Hamas said it remained committed to implementing the agreement and called on mediators to prevent violations. Netanyahu said discussions with US officials were continuing, but his public rejection underscores pressure from hardliners in his coalition and risks complicating Washington’s effort to broker regional settlements.
stories.headline: Israel rejects Trump’s 15-point Gaza plan, creating a rare public split with Washington

stories.body: Brent crude rose more than 1% to $84.43 a barrel after Iran said the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen without major US concessions, including sanctions relief and war reparations. The waterway, which carried about a fifth of global oil supplies before the conflict, has seen shipping collapse since the war began in late February: ship-tracking data showed only eight to 15 vessels crossing on several recent days, compared with roughly 130 before the conflict. Analysts said the absence of a concrete agreement was sustaining a risk premium in oil prices, even as Asian equity markets rose. Iran and Oman were said to be close to an understanding, but Tehran’s conditions and doubts about how any deal would work continued to unsettle markets.
stories.headline: Oil prices rise as Iran’s demands cloud the outlook for the Strait of Hormuz

stories.body: The global average sea-surface temperature outside polar regions reached its highest level on record for July, surpassing the previous July record from 2023, according to the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service. Record July sea temperatures were also recorded along the Atlantic coast and in the western Mediterranean, where severe marine heatwaves developed. Globally, July 2026 was effectively tied with July 2024 as the second-warmest July for surface air temperatures, while western Europe experienced its hottest June-July period on record. Copernicus said persistent heat and drought reinforced one another across the region, worsening wildfire conditions, reducing river flows and putting pressure on agriculture, water supplies and power plants.
stories.headline: World oceans recorded their hottest July temperature on record, scientists say

stories.body: Congressional Democrats have opened an investigation into the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement practices after the detention of dozens of spouses and parents of active-duty US service members. The cases followed the end of protections that had previously been available to military families, according to the Associated Press. The inquiry focuses on whether immigration actions affecting service members and their relatives undermine military readiness and the commitments made to those serving in the armed forces.
stories.headline: Congressional Democrats investigate efforts to deport US military personnel and their families

stories.body: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement says it expects to equip every field officer and agent with body cameras by the end of August or September, but its policy gives agency leadership broad discretion over public release of footage. The policy says recordings of encounters in which agents cause death or serious injury should be released promptly only when doing so is judged to be in the agency’s best interests. ICE says restrictions are intended to protect investigations and privacy and argues that the Associated Press mischaracterized the policy, while experts say the provision could permit selective disclosure in high-profile cases. The rollout follows heightened scrutiny after fatal ICE-involved shootings that were not captured on body cameras.
stories.headline: ICE policy says body-camera footage will be released only when it serves the agency’s ‘best interests’

stories.body: Wildfires and a heat dome brought evacuations and dangerous temperatures across western North America. In British Columbia, more than 20,000 people fled communities around Okanagan Lake as the fast-moving Bald Range wildfire destroyed homes; an 80-year-old woman died while trying to escape, and about 8,000 people were also evacuated around Peachland. In Washington state, crews continued work around fires near Spokane that had been burning for more than a week. Meanwhile, extreme heat stretched from Arizona to Montana, with Las Vegas reaching 115F, Phoenix forecast to reach 116F and El Centro, California, expected to hit 118F. Forecasters warned that the intense heat was increasing wildfire risk in already dry areas.
stories.headline: Wildfires and dangerous heat prompt evacuations across the western United States and Canada

stories.body: Thousands of people gathered in Ceuta’s Plaza de la Constitución under the slogan “Enough. Ceuta does not surrender,” calling for a stronger response to the territory’s migration crisis after a mass crossing from Morocco on 30 July. Organizers put attendance above 10,000, while police estimated a little more than 5,000; another report put the organizers’ figure above 15,000. The demonstration was convened by the city’s Christian, Muslim, Jewish and Hindu communities and emphasized coexistence and unity, while its manifesto asked Spanish and European authorities for resources, border attention, humanitarian assistance and a lasting solution. Ceuta’s president, Juan Jesús Vivas, said the situation was unsustainable and that the city could not face it alone.
stories.headline: Thousands demonstrate in Ceuta, demanding action over the migration crisis

stories.body: Spain has expanded spot document checks for travelers arriving from Italy to ports and airports across the country, retaliating after Italy imposed checks on travelers from Spain on 1 August in response to the Ceuta migration influx. Madrid said Italy’s measure was unjustified because Ceuta is outside the Schengen area and most people who entered had been returned to Morocco. Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, called Spain’s response incomprehensible and unacceptable, arguing that Italy had a duty to protect its borders. Spain’s Interior Ministry said its temporary controls were intended to address pressure on the central Mediterranean route and Italy’s alleged failure to comply with new EU asylum-responsibility rules; 199 third-country nationals arriving on 12 flights from Italy were checked on the first day.
stories.headline: Spain and Italy escalate their dispute over border controls affecting travelers

stories.body: Plans by Chinese electric-vehicle maker SAIC Motor to build its first European plant near the port of Ferrol have prompted concern within Spain’s defence and intelligence establishment because of its proximity to a strategically important naval base and Navantia shipyard. The project, expected to be operational in 2028, would help SAIC avoid EU tariffs on Chinese-made cars and is being promoted as a major investment for Galicia. But military sources warn that a Chinese industrial and shipping presence near the entrance to the estuary could expose information about Spanish naval movements, including F-100 Aegis frigates and the future F-110 frigates based or built in Ferrol, and could cause NATO and EU partners to question the port’s security.
stories.headline: Chinese EV plant planned beside Ferrol naval base raises security concerns

stories.body: Spain is preparing for a total solar eclipse on Wednesday, 12 August, the first total eclipse visible from the Iberian Peninsula since 1912. The path of totality will cross Galicia, Asturias, Castile and León, Aragon, the Valencian Community and the Balearic Islands late in the day, while the rest of the country will see a partial eclipse. Scientific teams are planning at least 10 projects across Spain, including observations of the solar corona by NASA and the European Space Agency, a new coordinated telescope network, atmospheric measurements and citizen-science studies of human and animal behavior. Authorities urge viewers to use certified ISO 12312-2:2015 solar-viewing glasses and proper filters for cameras, telescopes and binoculars.
stories.headline: Spain prepares for the August 12 total solar eclipse

stories.body: Western Europe has experienced its hottest start to summer on record, with June and July exceptionally hot and dry, according to Copernicus. June alone was Europe’s hottest recorded June, and sea temperatures were about 3C above average. The most severe conditions affected Spain, France, the United Kingdom and parts of Germany, where persistent heat and drought compounded one another by drying soils and reducing their natural cooling effect. Copernicus also reported record global July ocean temperatures of 20.96C and record sea-surface temperatures in the Atlantic and western Mediterranean. The heat and dryness helped drive record wildfire emissions, including Spain’s most severe recorded fire, which burned nearly 80,000 hectares across Ávila, Madrid and Toledo.
stories.headline: Copernicus confirms western Europe’s hottest summer on record

stories.body: Barcelona has opened 19 of the 41 libraries it manages during August, five more than last year, as part of a network of nearly 500 climate shelters. Residents in neighborhoods including Horta say this still leaves some districts without a nearby library where people can spend long periods escaping the heat. The Horta neighborhood association is calling for more than one library per district to remain open throughout the month, arguing that libraries offer not only air conditioning but also space to read, study, use the internet and spend time safely. The request follows a record-hot July in Catalonia and reflects growing reliance on public facilities during summer heatwaves.
stories.headline: Barcelona residents call for more libraries to remain open as climate shelters during August heat

stories.body: Barcelona’s beaches are seeing far fewer jellyfish this summer, a change experts link to exceptionally warm coastal waters. Jellyfish born near the coast may not have survived their early development stages, while open-sea species such as Pelagia noctiluca have found it more difficult to approach shore because coastal water is much warmer. Although the decline may make swimming easier for beachgoers, marine biologists say it is a worrying sign of the effects of ocean warming on the ecosystem. Josep Maria Gili of the Institute of Marine Sciences said jellyfish are a normal and necessary part of marine life and warned that the heat has become so intense that even they may not survive.
stories.headline: Exceptionally warm sea temperatures leave Barcelona with far fewer jellyfish this summer

stories.body: Catalonia’s government has received 12,143 objections to its PLATER plan for the territorial rollout of renewable energy, which is intended to guide decarbonization through 2050. The Territorial Planning, Housing and Ecological Transition Department described the response as a participation success and said the Catalan Energy Institute would assess proposals that are technically viable before opening a second public-consultation period. The plan has faced strong opposition from municipalities, local groups and farming organizations; opponents say the volume of objections shows it must be redesigned with greater local input. More than 300 councils are reported to oppose it, while the government says municipalities have already been able to reduce designated priority land for solar installations by 35% and that no municipality would be expected to devote more than 5% of its area to renewable generation by 2050.
stories.headline: Catalunya receives more than 12,000 objections to the PLATER territorial plan
